opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, because people often put UMI in a different bucket. When we say "robot data," we usually mean teleoperation: someone controls a real robot, and you record the robot's own sensors and joint commands. That data is tied to a specific robot and to the time and cost of running it.

UMI is different. It's a handheld gripper with a camera, like a GoPro, mounted on it. A person carries it around and does the task with their own hand, wiping a table, putting dishes away, whatever it is. No robot is involved during collection. The motion comes from a human arm, wrist, and body, with all the natural timing and corrections a person makes. So in terms of who produces the behavior, it really is human demonstration data.

What makes it clever is that the interface is designed so the data looks close to what a robot would see and do. The camera is mounted on the gripper, the robot has the same gripper and camera, and the action is the end-effector pose, which you can map onto a robot arm. It narrows the embodiment gap at the hardware level rather than leaving it all to the learning algorithm.

That's why I see it as one point on a spectrum of human data, not a separate category. At one end is passive human video, like YouTube or egocentric recordings: huge amounts of it, but hard to use directly because the embodiment differs so much. At the other end is teleoperation, which is very aligned with the robot but expensive and hard to scale. UMI sits in between. You give up some naturalness, since people hold a device instead of using bare hands. In return you get data that transfers to robots much more easily, while keeping the main advantage of human data: you can scale it without a robot in the loop. You can send devices into homes and kitchens and collect in places a robot would never go.

So my broader view is that we shouldn't treat human data versus robot data as a binary. The real question is how to design the collection interface and the learning methods together, so we can use the scale of human experience and still get policies that run on real robots. UMI is one good example of making that tradeoff on purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that what UMI gives you is still a human doing the task. The device itself is just a handheld gripper with a camera and some tracking on it, so you're not teleoperating a robot through some interface. You're actually using your own arm, your own wrist, your own sense of the physical world, and reaching out and grasping the object directly. So the motion, the timing, the way you adjust when something slips, all of that comes from a human's embodied intuition, not from a robot controller.

The gripper just happens to be shaped so that it roughly matches what the robot's end effector looks like. That's what makes the data transferable. But the intelligence behind it, the decision of where to go, how fast to approach, when to close the fingers, is entirely human. In that sense it's really a lot closer to something like egocentric human video than it is to robot data. The thing that's different from plain human video is that you get the action labels, the gripper pose and open-close state, in a form a robot can actually consume.

So I'd put it on a spectrum. On one end you have raw human video, which is abundant but has no clean action signal. On the other end you have robot data collected on the actual hardware, which is perfectly in-distribution but expensive and slow. UMI sits in between. It's cheap and natural to collect, like human data, because the person moves freely without the robot in the loop. And that's exactly why I consider it human data. The embodiment gap still exists. The robot can't move its arm exactly the way a human wrist can, and you still have to deal with that at deployment time. But the source of the behavior is a person, and that matters a lot for how you think about scaling it.

astra-6.text:
I consider it human data because the human is actually performing the task. With UMI, you’re holding a handheld gripper and interacting with the world, and we record that interaction. You decide where to grasp, how to move, how to respond when something slips—all of that behavior comes from you.

The gripper provides an interface that makes those demonstrations easier to transfer to a robot. So it’s not bare-hand human motion, but it’s still human-generated behavior. You’re demonstrating the skill directly, rather than operating a robot to collect the demonstration.

sol-6.1.text: I consider it human data because a human is still doing the task. UMI is an interface that lets us capture that demonstration in a form a robot can learn from. The person decides how to approach an object, where to grasp it, how to move it, and how to recover when something goes wrong. Those decisions and movements come from the human, even though they’re recorded through a device. So the interface makes the demonstration useful for robotics, but the behavior itself is human.
